questions.enonce_markdown:
A particle moves in a plane such that, at time $t$, its polar coordinates are $(r, \theta)$, where $r = 2t^2$ and $\theta = 3t$.

Find the speed of the particle when $t = 1$. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In polar coordinates the velocity has a radial component $\dot r$ and a transverse component $r\dot\theta$, perpendicular to each other, so the speed is $v = \sqrt{\dot r^2 + (r\dot\theta)^2}$.

With $r = 2t^2$ and $\theta = 3t$: $\dot r = 4t$, $\dot\theta = 3$, so $r\dot\theta = 6t^2$.

At $t = 1$: $\dot r = 4$ and $r\dot\theta = 6$.

$$
v = \sqrt{4^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13} \approx 7.21.
$$

The speed at $t = 1$ is $2\sqrt{13} \approx 7.21$ (in the units of the problem).

questions.enonce_markdown:
A particle moves on the curve with polar equation $r = 3e^{\theta}$ so that its radial component of velocity when it is at a distance $r$ from the pole is $\dfrac{2}{r}$.

Show that the acceleration of the particle is $\dfrac{8}{r^3}$ and is directed towards the pole. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radial component of velocity is $\dot r = \dfrac{2}{r}$.

Since $r = 3e^{\theta}$, differentiating with respect to time gives $\dot r = 3e^{\theta}\dot\theta = r\dot\theta$. Hence

$$
r\dot\theta = \frac{2}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dot\theta = \frac{2}{r^2}.
$$

Radial acceleration $= \ddot r - r\dot\theta^2$. Differentiate $\dot r = 2/r$:

$$
\ddot r = -\frac{2\dot r}{r^2} = -\frac{2}{r^2}\cdot\frac{2}{r} = -\frac{4}{r^3},
\qquad
r\dot\theta^2 = r\cdot\frac{4}{r^4} = \frac{4}{r^3}.
$$

$$
\text{radial acceleration} = -\frac{4}{r^3} - \frac{4}{r^3} = -\frac{8}{r^3}.
$$

Transverse acceleration $= \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(r^2\dot\theta\right)$. Here $r^2\dot\theta = r^2\cdot\dfrac{2}{r^2} = 2$, a constant, so the transverse acceleration is $0$.

The acceleration is therefore purely radial, of magnitude $\dfrac{8}{r^3}$, and the negative sign means that it is directed towards the pole.
